Basil of Caesarea. "De Spiritu Sancto (On the Holy Spirit)." Translated by Blomfield Jackson. In Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd ser., vol. 8. Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing, 1895. New Advent: Church Fathers. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3203.htm.

Basil's mature treatise (c. 375) on the Holy Spirit's equal glory with the Father and Son, written for Amphilochius of Iconium. Chapter 9.23 is the most famous deification text in Basil: through the Spirit souls are purified, become 'spirit-bearing' and radiant like transparent bodies struck by a sunbeam, pass their grace on to others, and reach 'the highest goal of all, becoming a god'. Russell reads it as social, eschatological and Spirit-centred rather than simply Plotinian. This is already in the owner's library (Jackson's NPNF translation, the one Russell uses); for a modern version see Stephen M. Hildebrand's translation, On the Holy Spirit (Popular Patristics 42, SVS Press, 2011, ISBN 978-0-88141-876-7). For the owner it is the core Cappadocian text for Spirit-encounter as transformation, purification of the passions, and a deification that overflows to others.

p. 209: De Sp. S. 9.23 (PG 32.109BC) is quoted at length (trans. Jackson, modified) as the most famous reference to human divine destiny in Basil; Russell notes its social character and argues, against Henry's Plotinian reading, for a Christian background (Hippolytus, Methodius, Clement).

p. 211: De Sp. S. 9.23 (PG 32.109AB): the Spirit makes human beings spiritual, conforms them to the image of the Son and raises them to the archetypal beauty, with first fruits in baptism and fulfilment only in heaven.

p. 211: De Sp. S. 1.2 (PG 32.69B): after glorifying God, the Christian aim is likeness to God as far as human nature allows; the telos is the blessed life of the age to come.

Annotated bibliography

Leemans, Johan, and Matthieu Cassin, eds. Gregory of Nyssa: Contra Eunomium III. An English Translation with Commentary and Supporting Studies. Translated by Stuart George Hall. Supplements to Vigiliae Christianae 124. Leiden: Brill, 2014.

Proceedings of the 12th International Colloquium on Gregory of Nyssa (Leuven, 2010), built around Stuart G. Hall's new English translation of Book III of Contra Eunomium, with commentary and studies. Book III (Jaeger's numbering; NPNF's 'Book V') includes Gregory's Christology of the transformation of Christ's humanity, with the same drop-of-vinegar-in-the-ocean image as the anti-Apollinarian works. Russell cites it beside those works for the mixture Christology behind deification. For the owner it is a scholarly entry into Nyssa's anti-Eunomian Christology, and a model of current Nyssa scholarship.

How it is used in Russell, The Doctrine of Deification in the Greek Patristic Tradition, ch. 7:

  • p. 229: C. Eunom. 3.4 (GNO II.150) is cited with the anti-Apollinarian texts for the image of humanity absorbed by the divine like a drop of vinegar in the ocean.

Annotated bibliography

Gregory of Nyssa. Anti-Apollinarian Writings. Translated by Robin Orton. The Fathers of the Church 131. Washington, DC: Catholic University of America Press, 2015.

The first published English translation of Gregory's Antirrheticus against Apollinarius and his letter To Theophilus, against the Apollinarians, with commentary. Both texts use Gregory's famous image of Christ's humanity absorbed into the divinity like a drop of vinegar in a boundless ocean, transformed and made incorruptible but still existing and still human. Russell uses them for the 'mixture' Christology that grounds Gregory's account of deification, and notes the anti-Apollinarian reasons for his reticence about deification language. For the owner it shows the Christological basis on which human nature can be transformed without being destroyed.

How it is used in Russell, The Doctrine of Deification in the Greek Patristic Tradition, ch. 7:

  • p. 229: Antirrh. 42 (GNO III/1.201) and Ad Theoph. adv. Apoll. (GNO III/1.126): the drop-of-vinegar-in-the-ocean image, which Russell uses to show that the humanity taken up into divinity is transformed but not annihilated.

Annotated bibliography

Gregory of Nyssa. Catechetical Discourse: A Handbook for Catechists. Translated by Ignatius Green. Popular Patristics Series 60. Yonkers, NY: St Vladimir's Seminary Press, 2019.

Gregory's Great Catechetical Oration (c. 385), a handbook for catechists on the Trinity, creation, fall, the Incarnation and the sacraments, here in Greek with a new English translation. Chapter 37 extends the deification of Christ's flesh to believers through the Eucharist: the God who mingled himself with mortal nature 'plants himself' in believers through his flesh, mingling with their bodies so that by union with the immortal they share in incorruption. Russell quotes it from Srawley (Greek text, Cambridge Patristic Texts, Cambridge University Press, 1903, whose pagination he cites). For the owner it is the classic patristic text on the transformation of the body through sacramental union, the most direct link between deification and bodily change.

How it is used in Russell, The Doctrine of Deification in the Greek Patristic Tradition, ch. 7:

  • p. 228: Or. Cat. 37 (PG 45.97B; Srawley 152.1) is quoted (trans. Srawley): by communion with the Godhead humanity is deified, Christ planting himself in believers' bodies through the Eucharistic flesh so they partake of incorruption.

Annotated bibliography

Gregory of Nyssa. The Lord's Prayer; The Beatitudes. Translated by Hilda C. Graef. Ancient Christian Writers 18. Westminster, MD: Newman Press, 1954.

Graef's translation, the one Russell uses, of Gregory's five homilies on the Lord's Prayer and eight on the Beatitudes, moral and spiritual sermons rather than allegorical exegesis. In the fifth homily on the Beatitudes Gregory says that through each beatitude the Lord 'deifies, so to speak' the hearer who understands rightly, since blessedness is the property of God and the merciful become gods by modelling themselves on God's mercy. Russell uses this as his main instance of deification by participation in the divine attributes, which he calls strictly analogous. For the owner it links deification to the daily practice of virtue and prayer, the ordinary, repeated side of encounter.

How it is used in Russell, The Doctrine of Deification in the Greek Patristic Tradition, ch. 7:

  • p. 227: De Beat. 5 (PG 44.1249A): through each beatitude the Lord 'deifies as it were' the hearer, and the merciful are invited to become 'a god'; Russell's example of deification by participation in divine attributes, qualified by τρόπον τινά.

Annotated bibliography

Winslow, Donald F. The Dynamics of Salvation: A Study in Gregory of Nazianzus. Patristic Monograph Series 7. Cambridge, MA: Philadelphia Patristic Foundation, 1979.

A study of Gregory of Nazianzus' soteriology, which Russell calls the most comprehensive study of deification in Gregory. Winslow treats theosis as a fluid, fundamentally metaphorical term for a dynamic relationship between God and humanity, 'our progressive growth towards an adopted dignity of fulfilled creatureliness', with six dimensions: spatial, visual, epistemological, ethical, corporate and social. Russell accepts this reading while questioning the weight Winslow gives to the corporate and social dimensions and his claim that Gregory went far beyond his predecessors. For the owner it offers a ready-made way to describe transformation as dynamic and many-sided, which fits encounter language well.

How it is used in Russell, The Doctrine of Deification in the Greek Patristic Tradition, ch. 7:

  • p. 224: Cited (1979: 189) for theosis as a fluid term for 'our progressive growth towards an adopted dignity of fulfilled creatureliness'; Russell endorses Winslow's sixfold dimension (193 ff.) but calls his claim (179) that Gregory went far beyond his predecessors an exaggeration.

Annotated bibliography

Gregory of Nazianzus. On God and Christ: The Five Theological Orations and Two Letters to Cledonius. Translated by Frederick Williams and Lionel Wickham. Popular Patristics Series 23. Crestwood, NY: St Vladimir's Seminary Press, 2002.

The standard modern English translation of the Theological Orations (Or. 27–31) and the Letters to Cledonius (Ep. 101–2), Gregory's defence of the Trinity and of Christ's full humanity. Oration 30 (the fourth theological oration) answers Eunomian proof-texts and ties deification to the Incarnation: 'What greater destiny can befall our humility than that humanity should be intermingled with God, and by this intermingling should become divine?' Russell uses it to show that for Gregory deification is incarnational at root and appropriated through baptism. For the owner it is the key Nazianzen text on the Incarnation as the ground of human transformation.

How it is used in Russell, The Doctrine of Deification in the Greek Patristic Tradition, ch. 7:

  • p. 221: Or. 30.3 is quoted: humanity 'intermingled with God' becomes divine; Russell's evidence that the incarnational context of deification is never lost sight of, the new deified humanity being appropriated through baptism.

Annotated bibliography

Gregory of Nazianzus. "Oration 2: In Defence of His Flight to Pontus." Translated by Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow. In S. Cyril of Jerusalem, S. Gregory Nazianzen, edited by Philip Schaff and Henry Wace. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd ser., vol. 7. Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing, 1894. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/310202.htm.

Gregory's apology (362) for fleeing to Pontus after his forced ordination, which became a classic treatise on the priesthood and the care of souls. In section 22 he states the pastor's aim: 'to give the soul wings', to make Christ dwell in the heart through the Spirit, and 'to deify' those who belong to heaven. Russell reads it as Platonic in its opening image but baptismal in its close: the priest deifies as spiritual guide and through the sacraments. For the owner it frames deification as pastoral and communal, the work of a spiritual guide, which fits a ministry-centred account of encounter.

How it is used in Russell, The Doctrine of Deification in the Greek Patristic Tradition, ch. 7:

  • p. 218: Or. 2.22 is quoted: the pastor's aim is to give the soul wings, make Christ dwell in the heart through the Spirit, and 'deify' those who have promised heavenly allegiance; Russell sees an oblique reference to baptism.

Annotated bibliography

Gregory Nazianzen and Ambrose. Funeral Orations by Saint Gregory Nazianzen and Saint Ambrose. Translated by Leo P. McCauley et al. The Fathers of the Church 22. New York: Fathers of the Church, 1953.

English translation of Gregory of Nazianzus' four funeral orations (on Caesarius, Basil, Gorgonia and his father) and Ambrose's oration on Satyrus, with an introduction on the Christian funeral oration. The oration on Caesarius (Or. 7, late 368 or early 369) describes the soul freed from 'the prison of this life', later receiving back the body that shared its philosophical life, and our becoming 'a son of God, a god myself' with Christ. Russell reads it as an early place where Pauline and Platonic strands of deification mingle, with deification tied to baptism. For the owner it speaks directly to body and soul: the body is not the prison, and it shares in the soul's final joy.

How it is used in Russell, The Doctrine of Deification in the Greek Patristic Tradition, ch. 7:

  • p. 217: The funeral oration for Caesarius (Or. 7.21–23): the soul escapes 'this life' and later shares its joys with the body; we linger in bodily tombs 'when we have become gods' (Ps 82:6); and 'a god myself' with Christ, read by Russell as Pauline and Platonic themes mingling.

Annotated bibliography

Gregory of Nyssa. Encomium of Saint Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa, on His Brother Saint Basil, Archbishop of Cappadocian Caesarea: A Commentary, with a Revised Text, Introduction, and Translation. Edited and translated by James Aloysius Stein. Catholic University of America Patristic Studies 17. Washington, DC: Catholic University of America, 1928.

Gregory of Nyssa's panegyric on his brother Basil (In laudem fratris Basilii, PG 46.788–817), delivered for Basil's feast after his death in 379, here in a revised Greek text with English translation and commentary by Sister James Aloysius Stein. Gregory compares Basil with Moses and other biblical saints who saw God. Russell's citation (PG 46.800D, 804BC, 808C) falls within this work and is used as evidence that Basil himself experienced the vision of God in this life. For the owner it is a rare patristic witness to a Cappadocian's own experience of divine encounter, not just his doctrine of it.

How it is used in Russell, The Doctrine of Deification in the Greek Patristic Tradition, ch. 7:

  • p. 212: PG 46.800D, 804BC, 808C: Russell says the vision of God may begin in this life (Moses, the disciples on Tabor) and that Basil himself had experience of this, 'as Gregory of Nyssa suggests in his encomium on his brother'.

Annotated bibliography

Silvas, Anna M. The Asketikon of St Basil the Great. Oxford Early Christian Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2005.

A full English translation of Basil's ascetic corpus, including the Longer Responses (Regulae fusius tractatae) and Shorter Responses, with studies of early monasticism in Asia Minor. At Longer Response 43.1 Basil defines Christianity as 'the imitation of Christ in the measure of his incarnation'. Russell uses it to show that Basil's way to likeness to God runs through mimesis and the practice of virtue more than through participation. For the owner it is the primary source for Cappadocian asceticism as the daily, embodied shape of transformation.

How it is used in Russell, The Doctrine of Deification in the Greek Patristic Tradition, ch. 7:

  • p. 211: Reg. fus. tract. 43.1 (PG 31.1028C): Basil's definition of Christianity as imitation of Christ's incarnate life, which Russell says enables us to fulfil our calling to become like God.

Annotated bibliography

Basil of Caesarea. Against Eunomius. Translated by Mark DelCogliano and Andrew Radde-Gallwitz. The Fathers of the Church 122. Washington, DC: Catholic University of America Press, 2011.

The first complete English translation of Basil's Adversus Eunomium (363–4), his early polemic against the Neo-Arian Eunomius, with Eunomius' Apology. Book III, on the Holy Spirit, is where Basil, in his undisputed works, uses θεοποιέω for the Christian's destiny: those 'called gods' are the perfect in virtue, perfection comes through the Spirit, so the Spirit who deifies must himself be God. Russell stresses that for Basil deification by grace is mutable, linked to baptism, and analogical rather than ontological. It gives the owner a precise Cappadocian text on Spirit, virtue and baptism, and on the limits Basil puts on 'becoming gods'.

How it is used in Russell, The Doctrine of Deification in the Greek Patristic Tradition, ch. 7:

  • p. 208: Adv. Eun. 3.5: Russell's evidence that 'gods' for Basil are the perfect in virtue, and that since perfection is through the Spirit, the Spirit must be divine ('how can that which lacks deity deify others?'), deification by grace being mutable and an effect of baptism.
  • p. 211: Adv. Eun. 3.2 (PG 29.660BC): cited for Basil's occasional participation language, that we are sanctified by participation in the holiness of the Spirit, which Russell says Basil subordinates to imitation.

Annotated bibliography

Athanasius and Didymus the Blind. Works on the Spirit: Athanasius's Letters to Serapion on the Holy Spirit and Didymus's On the Holy Spirit. Translated by Mark DelCogliano, Andrew Radde-Gallwitz, and Lewis Ayres. Popular Patristics Series 43. Yonkers, NY: St Vladimir's Seminary Press, 2011.

A modern English translation of Athanasius' Letters to Serapion (c. 359–60), the first sustained argument for the full divinity of the Holy Spirit, paired with Didymus the Blind's On the Holy Spirit. Athanasius' key move is that the Spirit who sanctifies and deifies cannot be a creature, because only God can make creatures partakers of God. Russell treats this as the unacknowledged source of Basil's pneumatological argument from deification. For the owner it is the point where deification becomes explicitly the work of the Spirit, which is the natural bridge between Orthodox theosis and a Pentecostal theology of Spirit-encounter.

How it is used in Russell, The Doctrine of Deification in the Greek Patristic Tradition, ch. 7:

  • p. 207: Russell says Basil's proof of the Spirit's divinity from his power to deify, in Adversus Eunomium (363–4), is an argument clearly drawn, without acknowledgement, from Athanasius' Letter to Serapion.

Cyril of Alexandria. A Commentary upon the Gospel According to S. Luke. Translated by R. Payne Smith. 2 vols. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1859.

Cyril's homilies on Luke, preserved largely in Syriac and translated in the nineteenth century. Homilies x–xi, on the baptism and the Spirit's descent, link receiving the Spirit with participation in the divine nature. It's directly relevant to Spirit baptism and the Jordan. In the public domain; the text is online at tertullian.org.

How it is used in Black, "The Church in the Eternal Purpose of the Triune God" (PhD thesis, 2016):

  • p. 214: n. 1339: with the Five Tomes, as evidence that Cyril joins partaking of the Spirit to theosis, though 'without such an emphasis on its experiential nature'.

Annotated bibliography

Cyril of Alexandria. Commentary on John. Translated by David R. Maxwell. Edited by Joel C. Elowsky. 2 vols. Ancient Christian Texts. Downers Grove, IL: IVP Academic, 2013–2015.

The first complete modern English translation of Cyril's great commentary, central for his theology of participation in the divine life through the Son and the Spirit (e.g. on John 1:9, 14:23 and 17). It's the most accessible way into Cyril's account of the Spirit's indwelling and believers' sharing in the Son's sonship.

How it is used in Black, "The Church in the Eternal Purpose of the Triune God" (PhD thesis, 2016):

  • p. ~208: In. Io. 1.9 (with Irenaeus and Athanasius) for the Spirit's work in constituting the church as Christ's.
  • p. ~213: In. Io. 10, on John 14:23 (ET 2:193–94): the Father and Son making their home in believers, for indwelling and Spirit baptism.

Annotated bibliography

Cyril of Alexandria. Dialogues sur la Trinité. Vol. 1, Dialogues I et II. Edited and translated by Georges Matthieu de Durand. Sources Chrétiennes 231. Paris: Cerf, 1976.

The critical Greek text with French translation of Cyril's Dialogues on the Holy and Consubstantial Trinity. In Dialogue I (407c), Cyril reads Ephesians 3:6 (σύσσωμος, 'concorporeal') as believers' union with God through faith, the 'mystical blessing' (the Eucharist), and the Spirit's sealing. It's the patristic anchor for an embodied, ecclesial account of theosis. No complete English translation exists.

How it is used in Black, "The Church in the Eternal Purpose of the Triune God" (PhD thesis, 2016):

  • p. 182–84: The key text of §6.1.1.1: Black uses Dial. Trin. I.407c to give the Apostolics' 'Body of Christ' theosis a concorporeal, Cyrilline locus (faith, Eucharist, Spirit).

data.title: Science and Spirit: A Critical Examination of Amos Yong’s Pneumatological Theology of Emergence
data.abstractNote: This paper is a critical examination of Amos Yong’s pneumatological use of emergence theory. In seeking to bridge the divide between the worldviews of science and Pentecostalism, Yong sees emergence theory as a fruitful mediating discourse. We will argue for the following: 1) the supernaturalism of Yong’s Pentecostal theology renders the concept of emergence obsolete; 2) the ontological independence of various types of spirits in Yong’s theology breaks his commitment to supervenience theory; and 3) Yong’s transference of scientific concepts into the normative discourse of theology is potentially problematic. These criticisms should be seen as a call for Yong to depart from emergence theory (and supervenience) in his admirable ambition to harmonize the spirit-filled imagination of Pentecostalism with the scientific culture of the 21st century.

Annotated bibliography

Suurmond, Jean-Jacques. “The Church at Play: The Pentecostal/Charismatic Renewal of the Liturgy as Renewal of the World.” In <i>Pentecost, Mission and Ecumenism: Essays on Intercultural Theology; Festschrift in Honour of Professor Walter J. Hollenweger</i>, edited by Jan A. B. Jongeneel, 247–59. Studien zur interkulturellen Geschichte des Christentums 75. Frankfurt am Main: Peter Lang, 1992.

An essay in the Hollenweger Festschrift by the Dutch charismatic theologian Jean-Jacques Suurmond, presenting charismatic worship as play that frees the church from goal-oriented, play-corrupting attitudes and so renews the world. It is a forerunner of his book <i>Word and Spirit at Play</i> (1994) and a key source for Vondey’s play thesis. For the owner it frames liturgy and encounter as non-instrumental, gratuitous participation, which resonates with Orthodox liturgical theology.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Religion as Play:

  • p. 9: Cited (Suurmond 1992, pp. 250–52) alongside Vondey 2010 for the contrast between Pentecostal affective spirituality and the performative, utilitarian and competitive character of traditional theology. (Also cited, unhighlighted, at p. 4.)

Some details unverified, see sources.json.

Annotated bibliography

Vondey, Wolfgang. <i>Beyond Pentecostalism: The Crisis of Global Christianity and the Renewal of the Theological Agenda</i>. Pentecostal Manifestos 3. Grand Rapids, MI: Eerdmans, 2010.

Vondey’s programmatic argument that Pentecostalism, understood through the category of play and the Pentecostal imagination, can help renew a global Christian theology in crisis, across topics from doctrine to liturgy and economics. It is the fuller statement behind the “Religion as Play” article. For the owner it supplies the theoretical frame (play against performance and competition) that Vondey applies to sanctification in <i>Pentecostal Theology</i> (where he cites it, unhighlighted, at p. 78 n. 93).

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Religion as Play:

  • p. 9: Vondey cites his own book (2010, pp. 13–15) for the contrast between the affective dimension of Pentecostal spirituality and the performative, functionalistic, rationalistic, utilitarian and competitive character of traditional theology.

Annotated bibliography

Land, Steven J. <i>Pentecostal Spirituality: A Passion for the Kingdom</i>. Journal of Pentecostal Theology Supplement Series 1. Sheffield: Sheffield Academic Press, 1993.

A foundational work of Pentecostal theology arguing that Pentecostal spirituality is best understood through the affections (gratitude, compassion, courage), integrated orthodoxy, orthopraxy and orthopathy, and oriented by an eschatological passion for the kingdom. It draws deeply on Wesley and on Eastern Christian sources. For the owner it is essential: it gives the language of affective transformation of the person in encounter, and Vondey also cites it in <i>Pentecostal Theology</i> (p. 103, unhighlighted).

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Religion as Play:

  • p. 8: Cited (Land 1993, pp. 131–64) for passion as the bridge between Pentecostal experience and doctrine, the encounter with God shaping the person’s disposition toward God’s passion for the world.

Annotated bibliography

Neumann, Peter D. <i>Pentecostal Experience: An Ecumenical Encounter</i>. Eugene, OR: Pickwick, 2012.

A study of what Pentecostals mean by “experience” of the Spirit, examining Pentecostal theologians’ accounts and bringing them into ecumenical dialogue with other Christian theologies of experience. Vondey uses it to define Pentecostal experience as encounter with the Spirit as recorded in Scripture and manifested at Pentecost. For the owner it is a careful conceptual treatment of the very term “encounter/experience” the project will need to define.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Religion as Play:

  • p. 7: Cited (Neumann 2012, p. 7) for the definition of Pentecostal experience as the encounter with the Holy Spirit recorded in Scripture and manifested at Pentecost in charismatic signs and wonders. (Also cited, unhighlighted, at pp. 100–61 for the ambiguity of ‘experience’.)

Annotated bibliography

Chandler, Diane J., ed. <i>The Holy Spirit and Christian Formation: Multidisciplinary Perspectives</i>. Christianity and Renewal – Interdisciplinary Studies. New York: Palgrave Macmillan, 2016.

A multidisciplinary edited volume on how the Holy Spirit forms Christians, with contributions from theology, biblical studies, psychology (for example Stephen Parker on psychological formation) and practice. Vondey cites it as a whole for the dynamic by which Pentecostal spirituality moves from experience to testimony, affections, practices and embodiment. For the owner it is a contemporary resource on Spirit-driven formation of the whole person, body and soul.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Religion as Play:

  • p. 6: Cited (Chandler 2016) for the current of Pentecostal spirituality, from experience to testimony to affections to practices to embodiment and back, as the development of doctrine in Pentecostalism.

Annotated bibliography

Vondey, Wolfgang. <i>People of Bread: Rediscovering Ecclesiology</i>. New York: Paulist Press, 2008.

Vondey’s ecclesiology built around the biblical and liturgical image of bread (companionship, bread of life, broken bread, one bread), describing the church as the “people of bread.” It is an ecumenical and eucharistic work. Vondey points to it for the claim that Christ’s eucharistic presence must also be realized through Pentecost, which gives the owner a Pentecostal-eucharistic link relevant to sacramental accounts of transformation.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Pentecostal Theology: Living the Full Gospel:

  • p. 100: Vondey cites his own book (n. 78, pp. 173–94) for the claim that the full realization of the eucharistic presence of Christ must also lead through Pentecost.

Annotated bibliography

Mühlen, Heribert. <i>Una Mystica Persona: Die Kirche als das Mysterium der Identität des heiligen Geistes in Christus und den Christen</i>. 2nd ed. Paderborn: Schöningh, 1967.

Mühlen’s major work of pneumatological ecclesiology: the church as “one person in many persons,” the identity of the one Holy Spirit in Christ and in Christians. The 1967 second edition (first 1964) adds a chapter on the Second Vatican Council’s teaching. For the owner it is a substantial (German-language) source on the Spirit as the personal bond between Christ and believers, close to Orthodox and patristic participation themes.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Pentecostal Theology: Living the Full Gospel:

  • p. 99: Cited (n. 67, pp. 216–86) for Mühlen’s view of Pentecost as the historical continuation of Jesus’s own corporeal, inner experience of the Spirit at his baptism.

Annotated bibliography

Vondey, Wolfgang. <i>Heribert Mühlen: His Theology and Praxis; A New Profile of the Church</i>. Lanham, MD: University Press of America, 2004.

Vondey’s own monograph (from his doctoral work) on the German Catholic theologian Heribert Mühlen, whose pneumatological ecclesiology and later leadership in the charismatic renewal produced a sacramental theology of Spirit baptism modelled on Jesus’s own baptism. It shows Vondey’s long-standing Catholic-Pentecostal ecumenical interest behind this chapter. For the owner it is the best English-language entry into Mühlen, a sacramental theologian of encounter and personal transformation.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Pentecostal Theology: Living the Full Gospel:

  • p. 98: Vondey cites his own study (n. 66, pp. 196–211) for Mühlen’s reinterpretation of the sacramental view, identifying the baptism of Jesus as the prototype of Spirit baptism. (He also cites it, unhighlighted, at n. 58, pp. 161–262.)

Annotated bibliography

Lederle, Henry I. <i>Treasures Old and New: Interpretations of “Spirit-Baptism” in the Charismatic Renewal Movement</i>. Peabody, MA: Hendrickson, 1988.

A standard typology of how Spirit baptism has been interpreted across the charismatic renewal: neo-Pentecostal (a distinct second experience), sacramental (release of a grace already given in initiation) and integrative approaches. Vondey uses it repeatedly in this chapter as a map of the options. For the owner it is the quickest way to place an Orthodox, sacramental-ascetic reading of encounter within the existing range of positions.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Pentecostal Theology: Living the Full Gospel:

  • p. 98: Cited (n. 65, pp. 124–38) for the charismatic movements among Lutherans, Reformed and Eastern Orthodox supporting a sacramental understanding of Spirit baptism.

Annotated bibliography

McDonnell, Kilian, and George T. Montague. <i>Christian Initiation and Baptism in the Holy Spirit: Evidence from the First Eight Centuries</i>. Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 1991.

A study of New Testament and patristic sources, Latin, Greek and Syriac, arguing that what charismatics call baptism in the Spirit belonged to normal Christian initiation in the early church. It works through the fathers of the first eight centuries text by text. For the owner it is a ready-made bridge from Pentecostal encounter to patristic sources, and a key text for any argument that Pentecostal experience is “catholic” in the ancient sense.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Pentecostal Theology: Living the Full Gospel:

  • p. 98: Cited (n. 62, pp. 316–42) for the Catholic view that Spirit baptism cannot be severed from Christian initiation but is an anointing received at water baptism.

Annotated bibliography

Suenens, Léon Joseph. <i>A New Pentecost?</i> Translated by Francis Martin. London: Darton, Longman and Todd, 1975.

Cardinal Suenens’s book-length theological endorsement of the Catholic charismatic renewal, translated from <i>Une nouvelle Pentecôte?</i>, by one of the leading figures of Vatican II. It reads the renewal as an inner awakening of the Spirit already given in the sacraments rather than a second outpouring “from outside.” For the owner it shows how a sacramental, patristically minded tradition absorbed Pentecostal encounter, a path an Orthodox-deification account might also take.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Pentecostal Theology: Living the Full Gospel:

  • p. 98: Cited (n. 61, pp. 80–81) for the Catholic stress that there are not two baptisms: Spirit baptism renews from within the latent power of the Spirit already given.

Annotated bibliography

“Malines Document I.” In <i>Presence, Power, Praise: Documents on the Charismatic Renewal</i>, vol. 1, <i>Continental, National, and Regional Documents</i>, edited by Kilian McDonnell, 13–70. Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 1980.

The first Malines Document, <i>Theological and Pastoral Orientations on the Catholic Charismatic Renewal</i> (prepared at Malines, Belgium, May 1974, under Cardinal Suenens, with Kilian McDonnell among the drafters), here cited from McDonnell’s three-volume documentary collection. It interprets baptism in the Spirit as a conscious release or renewal of the Spirit already given in baptism and confirmation. For the owner it is the authoritative Catholic sacramental reading of Pentecostal encounter, which is the most natural conversation partner for an Orthodox, sacramental account of deification.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Pentecostal Theology: Living the Full Gospel:

  • p. 98: Cited (n. 59) for the Catholic view of Spirit baptism as a conscious experience of the power of the Spirit given at water baptism.
  • p. 98: Cited again as “Ibid., 39–40” (n. 60) for Spirit baptism as a further realization or deepening of the gift received at baptism and confirmation, not an independent sacramental grace.

Some details unverified, see sources.json.

Annotated bibliography

Fee, Gordon D. “Baptism in the Holy Spirit: The Issue of Separability and Subsequence.” <i>Pneuma</i> 7, no. 1 (1985): 87–99. https://doi.org/10.1163/157007485X00076.

A much-discussed article in which the Pentecostal New Testament scholar Gordon Fee questions whether the doctrine of Spirit baptism as an experience separable from and subsequent to conversion can be grounded exegetically in Luke-Acts, while affirming the Pentecostal experience itself. It set off decades of debate on Pentecostal hermeneutics. For the owner it matters as the hinge question of whether encounter is a distinct later event or a dimension of the whole Christian life, which bears on comparisons with Orthodox initiation and theosis.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Pentecostal Theology: Living the Full Gospel:

  • p. 94: Cited (n. 42) for the Pentecostal argument for the separability and subsequence of Spirit baptism from water baptism (Fee being the principal critic of that argument).

Annotated bibliography

Gause, R. Hollis. <i>Living in the Spirit: The Way of Salvation</i>. Cleveland, TN: Pathway Press, 1980.

A Wesleyan-Pentecostal (Church of God, Cleveland) account of the order of salvation that places Spirit baptism within a sequence of repentance, justification, regeneration, adoption and sanctification, with the believer living in the Spirit from the first moment of faith. A revised and expanded edition was issued by CPT Press (2009/2010). For the owner it is the classic statement of the “crisis moments” model of transformation that Vondey both draws on and nuances.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Pentecostal Theology: Living the Full Gospel:

  • p. 92: Cited (n. 32, pp. 59–72) for the Pentecostal view of the Christian life as distinct crisis moments, with Spirit baptism as a second or third ‘blessing’ after conversion.

Annotated bibliography

Albrecht, Daniel E. <i>Rites in the Spirit: A Ritual Approach to Pentecostal/Charismatic Spirituality</i>. Journal of Pentecostal Theology Supplement Series 17. Sheffield: Sheffield Academic Press, 1999.

An ethnographic and ritual-studies analysis of worship in Pentecostal/charismatic congregations, identifying the rites, modes of sensibility (celebration, contemplation, ecstasy and so on) and the embodied “ritual field” of the service. Vondey relies on it throughout the chapter for ritual as the bedrock of sanctification and Spirit baptism. For the owner it is the key empirical study of how encounter happens bodily in worship and how ritual forms the person.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Pentecostal Theology: Living the Full Gospel:

  • p. 86: Cited (n. 9, pp. 179–89) for “praying through” as an embodied affection carried out in modes of celebration, contemplation, penitence, ecstasy or improvisation.
  • p. 103: Cited (n. 87, p. 215) for the transformations at Spirit baptism (praying for the Spirit becoming praying in the Spirit) as a consequence of empowerment.

Annotated bibliography

Warrington, Keith. <i>Pentecostal Theology: A Theology of Encounter</i>. London: T&T Clark, 2008.

A widely used systematic introduction to Pentecostal belief and practice, organized around the claim that Pentecostal theology is fundamentally a theology of encounter with God. Warrington surveys God, Spirit, church, Spirit baptism, healing, ethics and eschatology from that experiential centre. Its subtitle names the owner’s central category, so it is a natural primary reference for “encounter” as a theological (not only experiential) term.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Pentecostal Theology: Living the Full Gospel:

  • p. 86: Cited (n. 3, pp. 214–19) for prayer meetings, tarrying services and other corporate and individual forms of “praying through” as typical among Pentecostals.
  • p. 94: Cited (n. 43, pp. 99–106) for the Pentecostal claim that Spirit baptism is distinct from conversion, available for the full unfolding of the Christian life and mission.

Annotated bibliography

Parker, Stephen. “Holiness as Play: A Developmental Perspective on Christian Formation.” In <i>A Future for Holiness: Pentecostal Explorations</i>, edited by Lee Roy Martin, 312–32. Cleveland, TN: CPT Press, 2013.

A chapter by the Regent University psychologist Stephen Parker (author of <i>Winnicott and Religion</i>) arguing from developmental psychology that holiness is formed through play, that is, creative, relational and imaginative engagement, rather than through rule-keeping performance. It anticipates Vondey’s own “religion as play” thesis (the owner’s second reading). For the owner it links sanctification to human formation and growth, a psychological angle on the transformation of body and soul.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Pentecostal Theology: Living the Full Gospel:

  • p. 81: Cited (n. 105) for the claim that sanctification is play rather than performance: creative, imaginative, demanding, relational and participatory rather than solitary.

Annotated bibliography

Alexander, Bobby C. “Pentecostal Ritual Reconsidered: Anti-Structural Dimensions of Possession.” <i>Journal of Ritual Studies</i> 3, no. 1 (1989): 109–28.

A ritual-studies article that applies Victor Turner’s categories of liminality and anti-structure to Pentecostal spirit possession, arguing that ecstatic worship enacts a real (not merely compensatory) transformation of status and community. Alexander later expanded this Turnerian reading in <i>Victor Turner Revisited</i> (1991). For the owner it offers an anthropological vocabulary for how encounter in worship reshapes the person bodily and socially.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Pentecostal Theology: Living the Full Gospel:

  • p. 79: Cited (n. 98, esp. pp. 113–16) for the claim that sanctification as ritual carries ontological rather than doctrinal or functional status.

Annotated bibliography

Macchia, Frank D. “Justification and the Spirit: A Pentecostal Reflection on the Doctrine by Which the Church Stands or Falls.” <i>Pneuma</i> 22, no. 1 (2000): 3–21. https://doi.org/10.1163/157007400X00024.

Macchia’s 2000 Society for Pentecostal Studies presidential address, an early form of the argument he later developed in <i>Justified in the Spirit</i> (2010, already in the owner’s library). It reframes justification pneumatologically, so that being put right with God is inseparable from the Spirit’s transforming indwelling. It matters to the owner because it gives a Pentecostal route from forensic justification toward participation and transformation, close to the Orthodox emphasis Vondey highlights.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Pentecostal Theology: Living the Full Gospel:

  • p. 79: Cited (n. 94, p. 19) for the claim that the Pentecostal perspective is closer to the Orthodox view of transformational practices that bridge Word and sacrament.

Annotated bibliography

Butler, Anthea D. “Observing the Lives of the Saints: Sanctification as Practice in the Church of God in Christ.” In <i>Practicing Protestants: Histories of Christian Life in America, 1630–1965</i>, edited by Laurie F. Maffly-Kipp, Leigh E. Schmidt, and Mark Valeri, 159–76. Baltimore, MD: Johns Hopkins University Press, 2006.

A historical chapter on the Church of God in Christ that treats sanctification not as a doctrine but as a set of observed, embodied practices: discipline of the body, prohibitions, fasting, prayer and communal oversight. Butler shows how Sanctified church members made holiness visible in daily life. For the owner it is a concrete, lived-religion account of bodily asceticism inside Pentecostalism, a good counterpart to Orthodox ascetic practice and to the theme of daily encounter.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Pentecostal Theology: Living the Full Gospel:

  • p. 78: Cited (n. 91; highlighted twice) for the claim that personal discipline is reinforced by communal prayer, revival meetings, fasting practices and ritual celebrations of the congregation.

Annotated bibliography

Bundy, David. “Visions of Sanctification: Themes of Orthodoxy in the Methodist, Holiness, and Pentecostal Traditions.” <i>Wesleyan Theological Journal</i> 39, no. 1 (2004): 104–36.

David Bundy’s Wesleyan Theological Society presidential address, tracing Eastern Christian (Orthodox) themes in the understanding of sanctification through the Methodist, Holiness and Pentecostal traditions. It supports the genealogical claim that the Wesleyan-Holiness stream in Pentecostalism inherits, through Wesley, patristic and Eastern notions of growth in holiness. For the owner it offers the historical bridge between the Cappadocian/Orthodox world and Pentecostal sanctification, rather than only a typological comparison.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Pentecostal Theology: Living the Full Gospel:

  • p. 77: Cited (n. 89; footnote highlighted twice) for the claim that Pentecostal theology, particularly its Wesleyan-Holiness tradition, stands in a certain continuity with the Orthodox view of sanctification.

Annotated bibliography

Rybarczyk, Edmund J. <i>Beyond Salvation: Eastern Orthodoxy and Classical Pentecostalism on Becoming Like Christ</i>. Carlisle: Paternoster, 2004.

A comparative monograph setting Eastern Orthodox theosis beside classical Pentecostal spirituality on the shared theme of becoming like Christ. Rybarczyk treats each tradition’s anthropology, means of grace (liturgy, sacraments, ascetic practice versus revival, piety and discipline) and vision of transformation, arguing for real if unacknowledged affinities. This is probably the single most important source in this reading for the owner: it sits exactly at the junction of Pentecostal encounter, Orthodox deification and ascetic practice, and Vondey leans on it twice in one paragraph.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Pentecostal Theology: Living the Full Gospel:

  • p. 77: Cited (n. 87, pp. 127–71) for the Orthodox means of sanctification-as-deification: participation in the church’s liturgy, sacraments and ascetic practices.
  • p. 77: Cited again (n. 90, pp. 271–323) for the Pentecostal ‘tributaries’ of sanctification (ritual practices, revivals, personal piety and ascetic discipline) that parallel the Orthodox view.

Annotated bibliography

Aden, Ross. “Justification and Sanctification: A Conversation between Lutheranism and Orthodoxy.” <i>St Vladimir’s Theological Quarterly</i> 38, no. 1 (1994): 87–109.

An article bringing the Lutheran distinction between justification and sanctification into conversation with the Orthodox refusal to separate them, by Ross (now Archpriest Basil) Aden, who has written on Orthodox readings of Luther and on “justification and divinization.” Vondey uses it for the claim that in Orthodoxy sanctification is ontological participation in the divine life, integrated with justification in the deifying transformation of the Christian. It is directly on the owner’s Orthodox-deification thread and helps frame how a Pentecostal account of transformation can avoid the forensic/transformative split.

data.title: Religion as Play: Pentecostalism as a Theological Type
data.abstractNote: This article suggests that Pentecostalism constitutes a genuine type of religion we can label as play. In order to identify the particular elements of this type, the article makes use of Erving Goffman’s frame analysis to organize Pentecostal theological activity. This methodological starting point is followed by an overview of existing interpretations of Pentecostalism as a form of play. The main portion of this essay then constructs from an analysis of everyday experiences visible in Pentecostalism a primary framework of activities oriented around the transformative encounter with the Holy Spirit. The sequence of activity involves a primary and overlapping pattern of Pentecostal spirituality, experience, narrative, affections, practices, and embodiment. Demonstrating that play is not exclusive to Pentecostalism, but that Pentecostals manifest a particularly visible form, demands that greater attention is paid both to Pentecostalism as a religious tradition and to play as a theological model.

Zizioulas states the three basin meanings for a person are 'a cry for defintion (who)', 'a cry for fixed being (am), and 'a cry for particularity (I)'. "In God it is possible for the particular to be ontologically ultimate because relatinship is permanent and unbreakable (i)" (41) Particularity and relatinship then coincide to produce being. Ultimately, Zizioulas is concenerd with the 'why' question (ousia/ubstance) not being answered by the 'what' (particular characteristics). For this brings being into a place that can be shared by others and does not point to absolute uniqueness. Who are you? I am a man studying at St. Andrews. This does not point to the 'who' of me. My identity/ousia is just in 'me' and that I am not someone else. He writes, "The true ontongoly of hyspostasis: that someone simply is (i) and is himself (i) and not someone else, and this is sufficient to identify him as being in the true sense. Thus there is no positive quality that can be given to a hypostasis/person for this would lose absolute particularity. The true personal identity of God and person then can only be seen through relationship and not through isolated ontology. 

Zizioulas starts from Greek philsophy for personhood and his three earlier questions of "who am I?' He then moves to the Cappodocian definitions of being through arche/beginning. Finally he ends in his thesis that ultimate particularity must be in pure being of someone, not in descriptions given to him. Is this what Christ taught us? I need to see if I agree with this or not.

data.abstractNote:
In human existence nature preceedes the person and thus a person is never the totality of human nature. One human cannot represent all humans, just as one human dies everyone does not die. They do not share the same 'substance', if you will. Thus, humans "as an entity [are] independent ontologically from other human beings" (48). God, on the other hand existsts outside beginning and time and there is no common divine nautre prior to the persons of the Tinirty, like humans. Equally, "and for the same reasons it is impossible to say that in God any of the three persons exist or can exist in separation from the other person. The three constitute such an unbreakable unity that individualism is absolutely inconceivable in their case" (48). (I'm not sure I see the connection between nature not preceeding divine persons and thus that logically leading to their unbreakable relationship). THis all came about through the Cappodocians against Sabellianism.

Secondly, against Eunomianism, there arose a sharp distinction between God's substance and person. This was to combat Eunomius who placed the substance of God in his unbegotteness, and said Jesus was not of the same substance becuase he was begotten. Here, Zizioulas remarks nothing at all can be said of the substance of God, except that it is one and undivided (49). Thus, Fatherhood and unbegotteness are "hypostatic properties" that are incomunicable to the other persons of the Trinity (49). Because any property that can be communicated can be shared, like a common substance or nature. The substance, 'oneness, is communicated between the divine persons, yet hypostatic properties are not. Personhood then becomes known through "its absolute uniqueness and irreplaceability, something that has not ceased to be of existential relevance in philosophy" (50). Zizioulas seeks to divorce neccesity or servitude of divine personhood to sibstance, which applies unaminously to created existence (50). 

Greek thought believed there was an ideal humanity "whoe image every human being is" or participates in" (53). Because of this human persons was neccesitated by its nature. It had to participate in the idael humanity or emerging out of the common human species. Nature always precedded the person. The Cappadocians saw the neccesity of nature being bound to their createdness. The only true being is found in the uncreated God whose existence does not prioritize the neccessary nature (oneness) over the many (particularities). Instead, "God exists simulatneously the 'one' and the 'Many, and this means that the person has to be given ontological primacy in philsophy" (53). 

Futhering on this, the Cappadocians linked true being to freedom, onr that does not exist neccesarily. Again overthrowing popular Greek thought, the world's being (and God's) is found in the frredom of the arche of the Father. God is the one Father who 'causes' the Son and the Spirit in freedom. THis is an act of love, and thus God is love. Existence then becomes free from logical necesity of substance (55).

When referring to human nsature, he refers to the 'substance; that is shared by all human beings (55). There is nothing unique about having this human nature. Humans can then decide to live towards their nature, as individuals that share nature, or live towards the image of God, who is an act of community. This is "an image of God's personhood" (55). 

In order to be yourself as a person, you must be free from anyy necessity: moral, religious or ideaological (56). "Nature always points to the general; it is the person that safeguards uniqueness and absolute particularity" (57). For nature is common and often neccesary, while persons are free, unique, and unrepeatable. 

Zizioulas then separates individuals from persons, for indvidiauls are taken from nature and "are never absolutely unique". They can be similar, combined with others to produce results or new species; they can be used to serve purposes. But persons can never be reproduced "nor perpetuated like species; they cannot be composed or decomposed, combined or used for any object whatsoeve" (57). Where does this come from? I need more research here. Whenever a person is treated this way, towards their substance, they dissolve them into non-eistence his "personal particularity (i)" (58). "Only when nature is hypostatic ot personal, as is the case with God, does it exist trully and eternally" (58). 

Father, Son, and Spirit are "indicative of personal (i) identity" (59) "And since these are the only (i) names that indicate personal identity they cannot be changed" (59). Father denotes person, while fatherly charactersitcs "are not personal (i) properties - they apply to  all three persons of the Trinity, i.e. to the common substance or energy" (60). God revlead himself in these personally particular names, and these should never change.
